lines.text: This is the ABC incident data sheet. One sheet records one incident of the target behavior: what was in place right before it, what the student did, and what followed. The behavior analyst enters each sheet into the record, where the analysis is built. Here is how to fill it out.

At the top, the student and the target behavior are printed for you. Write your name as the observer, the setting, the date, the start time, how many minutes the incident lasted, the activity or routine, and the names of the staff who were present.

Below that, mark whether an adult was within view, and circle the peak intensity, from one, minimal, to five, a crisis. The consequence window and the check interval are printed from the record. Use the ones printed on your sheet.
The middle of the sheet has three columns: antecedent, behavior, and consequence. Tick what you saw, not what you think the student wanted. Leave a box blank when it did not apply.
Here is an incident, filled in. Earlier in the day the student came in short of sleep, so that setting event is ticked on the row above the columns.

The antecedent is what was in place immediately before the behavior. The teacher put a math sheet on the desk and the work was difficult, so academic demand and difficult task are ticked in the first column.

In the middle column, tick the target behavior you saw. The student's own target behaviors, defined on Form TB-1, are printed first with their definitions; here, screaming and crying. Under preceded by, tick the lower intensity responses in the seconds before it: the student refused, then pushed the sheet away.
The consequence is what adults and peers did within the window, whether or not it was meant. The teacher took the sheet back, so demand removed is ticked in the third column.

Then write a brief description, in order, with the times: what was said, what the student did, what the adults did next, and how it ended. The codes carry the arithmetic; your words carry what the codes leave out.
At the bottom, tick what happened right after the consequence, and how the incident was resolved. Then hand the sheet in. One incident, one sheet.

The second sheet is the background sample. At each check of the timer when the behavior is not happening, you record what was in place anyway. Without these checks, the analysis cannot tell a trigger from something that is simply there all day.

Write the date, the time, and the activity. Tick the antecedent conditions in place at the check, and anything that happened in the seconds scored. Here the student was working on math with an adult within view, and nothing else happened.

Leave every box blank when none applied. An empty check is still data: it is what makes the base rate meaningful. Skip the check only when the behavior itself occurred in the seconds scored; that window is an incident.

In the record, the analysis puts the two sheets together. In this example, academic demand was in place before nine of twelve incidents, seventy-five percent, but in only four of twenty background checks, twenty percent. Demand goes with the behavior far more often than it is simply there.

The same comparison is made for every antecedent and every consequence, and the hypotheses are ranked for the functional analysis. It is a ranking, not a function statement, and the contingency strength is read only once ten or more background samples are on file.
A sample sheet is attached, marked SAMPLE across it. It shows how a finished sheet looks. It is not the student's data: do not count it or copy it. Fill in a blank sheet for each incident.
Thank you. Hand your sheets to the behavior analyst at the end of the day, with the background samples from the same session.
